title: NCR Patterns at ADW
body: The NCR corpus isn't random — it clusters at Stage 4, Stage 6, and the ROM pad, and at the exact hours supervision is thinnest. Ignore that pattern and you keep writing up the same failure mode in a new location instead of fixing the coverage gap that causes it.
keyPoints: Eight of nineteen NCRs sit at Stage 4, five at Stage 6, two at the ROM pad — the highest-stakes ground is also where supervision coverage is weakest. Treat that overlap as a staffing problem, not bad luck.

Incidents cluster at shift transitions: pre-dawn (04:00-06:30) before day shift supervisors are on site, and late day shift (16:00-17:20) when handover focus pulls supervisors off the floor. Build deliberate presence into those windows, don't assume the roster covers it.

"Refuse the truck" incidents (Galih, Syukur) share one gap: no formal verify-before-refuse step. An operator citing a defect from memory, without re-inspecting equipment that's since been repaired, costs production in the hundreds to low-thousands of tons per shift. Close that gap with a mandatory joint inspection before any refusal is accepted.

People NCR'd once often resurface as supervisors later (Sadiq Ali, John Konneh). That can be the process working — correction into responsibility — or it can be forced rotation covering a manpower gap. Don't assume either; check which one it actually is before relying on it.
A control that exists on paper but isn't spot-checked isn't a control — the WL-24 walkaround fix only holds if supervisors actually verify the signed checklist weekly, not just file it.
apply: If you're near Stage 4, Stage 6, or the ROM pad during a shift transition, that's exactly the coincidence this pattern predicts — make sure a supervisor is actually there, not just rostered to be.
